Good neighbors make lasting memory
abstract: A population of inflammatory monocytes differentiates into persistent lung-resident Gal-1+ myeloid cells that colocalize with and support the long-term maintenance and recall responses of influenza virus-induced tissue-resident memory CD8+ T cells.

title: Monocyte-derived galectin-1hi cells provide innate immune help in the generation of functional memory CD8+ T cells
abstract: After viral infections, tissue-resident memory T cells (T RM cells) are generated and reactivated rapidly upon re-exposure to previously encountered viral pathogens, providing immediate immune effector functions to limit infection at the site of viral entry. Here we found that a subset of newly recruited CCR2 + monocytes differentiated into memory-stage CCR2-tdTomato + cells and persisted in the lung for more than 4 months after infection with the influenza virus. Selective depletion of the memory-stage CCR2-tdTomato + cells reduced significantly the formation of lung CD8 + T RM cells and compromised secondary heterosubtypic immune protection. Memory-stage CCR2-tdTomato + cells colocalized with lung CD8 + T RM cells and secreted galectin-1, which activated CD8 + T cells directly and enhanced transforming growth factor-β sensing. Intranasal administration of recombinant galectin-1 as an adjuvant for the influenza vaccine induced superior memory CD8 + T cell responses. Thus, the presence of a unique memory-like monocyte-derived subset provided crucial signals to establish and maintain functional CD8 + T RM cells in the lung.

title: Immune-mediated rheumatoid arthritis: from single-cell genomics to new therapies
abstract: The recent application of single-cell genomics to the investigation of immune-mediated arthritis has resulted in an explosion of information, including the discovery of lymphocyte, myeloid and fibroblast cell subsets proposed to be pathogenic. A challenge in the field is how to leverage these exciting but largely descriptive and correlative datasets to gain insights into causality and mechanisms of disease. In this Perspective, I describe emerging data and discuss ideas about how spatial transcriptomics, ex vivo mechanistic and organoid studies, and improved use of animal models based on human disease data can advance the understanding of immune-mediated arthritis pathogenesis, with a focus on rheumatoid arthritis. These insights can form the basis for designing new therapeutic strategies and implementing clinical trials. The concepts and approaches described here for arthritis may have broader applicability to other tissues and immune-mediated diseases.

title: Innate immune imprints shape HIV-1 reservoir cell persistence during long-term antiretroviral therapy
abstract: Host immune responses that can target and eliminate HIV-1 reservoir cells during suppressive antiretroviral therapy are poorly understood. Here, analyzing over 6,000 proviral DNA amplicons from 104 individuals on long-term antiretroviral therapy, we found that carriers of HLA-C2 allotypes, which promote NK cell education via interactions with KIR2DL1, exhibited lower frequencies of intact proviruses. No protective effects of HLA-C2 alleles were observed during untreated infection, suggesting a selective vulnerability of reservoir cells to NK-cell-mediated immune activity under antiretroviral therapy. Supporting this, frequencies of KIR2DL1 + NK cells, particularly those coexpressing the activating HLA-E receptor NKG2C, were inversely correlated with frequencies of intact proviruses. Moreover, viral protein U variants that strongly downregulate HLA-C, increasing a missing-self response by KIR2DL1 + NK cells, were associated with smaller reservoirs in carriers of HLA-C2. Infected cells surviving long-term displayed elevated HLA-C expression, consistent with in vivo selection for resistance to KIR2DL1 + NK-cell-mediated immune clearance. Immune activity of KIR2DL1 + NK cells against viral reservoir cells was enhanced by NKG2C–HLA-E interactions, as sequence variants in HLA-E-restricted HIV-1 epitopes reduced NKG2C-dependent NK cell activation and were associated with higher frequencies of intact proviruses. These findings underscore the critical influence of host and viral genetic variation on reservoir persistence and highlight opportunities for leveraging innate immunity in HIV cure strategies.

title: Natural killers blast HIV reservoir landscape
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells leave distinct footprints on the HIV reservoir, leading to a smaller HIV reservoir size in individuals carrying the HLA-C2 allele. HIV escapes NK cell-mediated immunity through mutations in the viral proteins Vpu, Gag and Env.

title: Author Correction: Peyer’s patch M cells organize an epithelial niche that sustains group 3 innate lymphoid cells and IL-22
abstract: In the version of the article initially published, Matthew E. Ritchie’s surname appeared incorrectly (as Richie) and has now been amended in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

title: New frontiers in pathogen immunity
abstract: The EMBO workshop ‘Pathogen Immunity and Signaling’ was held from 8 to 11 June 2026 in Leiden, the Netherlands, bringing together 175 participants from 25 countries to discuss the latest advances in antimicrobial immune defense.

title: Intratumoral T cell activation kills tumors regardless of T cell specificity
abstract: Immunotherapies putatively require tumor-specific T cells. Here we show how T cells can eliminate tumors without tumor specificity via paracrine signaling. Activating unexhausted bystander non-tumor-specific T cells within tumors resulted in tumor elimination without conventional recognition-dependent mechanisms and in the absence of any tumor-specific T cell receptor (TCR)αβ + T cells. Robust T cell activation recruited immune cells, used innate leukocytes and triggered a tumoricidal combination of effector molecules and panoptotic pathways. Mechanistically, interferon-γ, tumor necrosis factor and nitric oxide induced caspase-dependent death, recapitulating melanoma clearance in mice or human melanoma cell death in vitro. Gene expression signatures associated with this response in mice were predictive of survival among human patients with melanoma. Thus, triggering productive T cell activation within tumors can be sufficient for immunotherapy, without needing to induce or rescue cancer-specific responses.

title: The dual roles of uterine monocytes in regulation of tissue homeostasis throughout reproductive cycles in health and disease
abstract: Inflammation occurs during the recurring cycles of tissue degradation, repair and remodeling in the uterus, but the mechanisms by which the immune system contributes to uterine tissue integrity are unclear. We reveal that uterine monocytes have dual roles in both tissue remodeling and inflammation, depending on the reproductive cycle stage. Circulating inflammatory monocytes infiltrated the uterus before their differentiation into proinflammatory or pro-repair macrophages, depending on interferon-γ and transforming growth factor-β, respectively. Human monocyte numbers peaked before the window of implantation, when an inflammatory environment is required for embryo implantation. Uterine monocytes exhibited cytotoxic properties, regulating epithelial cell apoptosis. Bioinformatic analyses of receptor–ligand interactions indicated that monocytes dominated interactions between myeloid cells and fibroblasts. These pathways were disrupted in uterine fibrosis, marked by excess inflammatory monocytes or macrophages and a loss of rhythmicity through reproductive cycles. These data reveal a key role for monocytes and their progeny in the regulation of uterine tissue homeostasis.

title: Neutrophil-hybrid CAR-macrophages bring double trouble to tumors
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) have revolutionized engineered cell therapies for cancer. Impressive anti-tumor effects have now been achieved by fitting CARs onto fused macrophage–neutrophil hybrid syncytial, with a promising outlook for stand-alone and combination therapies.

title: ID2 orchestrates the final ‘E-scape’ from the −165-kb Zeb2 enhancer for cDC1 specification
abstract: The Zeb2 −165-kb enhancer is not a simple genetic switch but a regulatory crossroads where transcription factors compete to calibrate lineage decisions and shape immune cell diversity.

title: AMBRA1 allosterically activates NLRP3 by releasing its autoinhibition
abstract: Nod-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) is activated by many stimuli, and its dysfunction is involved in various inflammatory diseases. Activation of NLRP3 is thought to happen via a multistep process involving phase separation, conformational opening and oligomerization. However, how NLRP3 is released from its autorepressed conformation remains elusive. Here we report that activating molecule in Beclin1-regulated autophagy protein 1 (AMBRA1), previously known for its role in autophagy, bound NLRP3 to scaffold and allosterically activate NLRP3. AMBRA1 engaged the leucine-rich repeat and helical domain 2 subdomains of NLRP3 through its β-propeller domain and destabilized the closed, inactive conformation of NLRP3, facilitating adenosine triphosphate binding and transition of NLRP3 to the active state. AMBRA1 deficiency in monocytes or macrophages impaired NLRP3 activation and reduced inflammatory responses in mouse models of endotoxic shock, colitis and sepsis. Nanobodies blocking the interaction between AMBRA1 and NLRP3 inhibited NLRP3 activation, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting this interaction. Our study revealed the role of AMBRA1 in NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activation, offering potential pharmacological targets for related diseases.

title: Microbial adhesion promotes Piezo1 activation to initiate innate immunity
abstract: How mammals mount an effective immune response against infectious agents remains unresolved. Here we identify microbial adhesion to myeloid cells as a critical initiating event that precedes pattern recognition receptor (PRR) engagement. Using a skin infection model with pathogenic bacteria and fungi, we demonstrate that neutrophil recruitment occurs in two sequential phases. The early phase is PRR-independent and instead driven by microbial adhesion, which engages the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 to promote leukotriene (LT)B 4 production. Together with interleukin-1α, LTB 4 induces CXCL1 release, triggering neutrophil infiltration via the same circuit at play during sterile inflammation. By contrast, the late phase is toll-like receptor (TLR)- and CXCL2-dependent, marking a transition to the canonical, pathogen-driven response. Our findings uncover microbial adhesion as a previously unrecognized danger signal that activates innate immunity via mechanotransduction, revealing a paradigm of how immune responses to infection are initiated.

title: The overlooked plasticity of monocytes in uterine homeostasis
abstract: Myeloid cell immunophenotyping in women and functional studies in mice indicated that monocytes contribute to both inflammation and tissue remodeling in the uterus and dynamically regulate tissue homeostasis throughout the reproductive cycle. Dysregulation of monocyte function was associated with uterine fibrosis (Asherman’s syndrome), which has severe consequences for reproductive health.

title: CD8+ T cells kill tumors by proxy
abstract: We found that antiviral CD8+ T cells can deputize the local innate immune system to destroy tumors. Thus, CD8+ T cells can kill by proxy, which has ramifications for cancer treatment and general mechanisms of CD8+ T cell function.

title: Dendritic cells sense microbial adhesion to launch innate immunity
abstract: In a mouse skin infection model, microbial adhesion to CD11c+ myeloid cells activates PIEZO1 and an LTB4–IL-1α–CXCL1 cascade that recruits neutrophils before Toll-like receptor signaling becomes dominant. These findings identify a first phase of innate immune defense that is driven by mechanical signals.

title: Author Correction: A novel CAF population coordinates hyper-suppressive regulatory T cell recruitment and localization in lung cancer
abstract: In the version of the article initially published, in the second paragraph of the “CXCR3 deficiency limits T reg cell trafficking and tumor growth” section, the text “Interestingly, tumors in mice with Cxcr3 -sufficient T reg cells exhibited a higher T conv :T reg ratio” should have read “Interestingly, tumors in mice with Cxcr3 -deficient T reg cells exhibited a lower T reg :T conv ratio”. This correction has been made to the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

title: ANKRD11 deficiency reprograms CD8+ T cell differentiation to enhance immunity in chronic infection and cancer
abstract: CD8 + T cell dysfunction is a major obstacle to hepatitis B virus (HBV) clearance and antitumor immunity. Here, using a humanized mouse model, we identify a T cell receptor targeting a clinically relevant HBV epitope and reveal ANKRD11 as a key epigenetic regulator of CD8 + T cell dysfunction in chronic infection and tumors. Ankrd11 knockout in CD8 + T cells enhances HBV-specific T cell proliferation and effector differentiation, especially under immunosuppressive conditions, via AP-1 family gene upregulation. Loss of Ankrd11 both drives the conversion of progenitor exhausted T cells into terminally exhausted T cells, and reprograms PD-1 − TOX − tolerant cells into functional effectors, improving antiviral and antitumor responses. Ankrd11 -deficient T cells show increased granzyme and superior effector function, enhancing viral control and tumor regression. These findings position ANKRD11 as a promising immunotherapy target for chronic HBV infection and cancer.

title: Dan Kastner (1951–2026)
Author Correction: The transcription factor TCF-1 initiates the differentiation of TFH cells during acute viral infection
Spatiotemporal single-cell profiling reveals T cell clonal dynamics and phenotypic plasticity in human graft-versus-host disease
abstract: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation cures hematologic diseases but is limited by acute graft‑versus‑host disease. How human T cell clones drive epithelial injury remains poorly mapped. We studied 31 transplant recipients, integrating longitudinal T cell antigen receptor (TCR) profiling with single-cell RNA sequencing/TCR sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to track T cell clonal dynamics. We developed DecompTCR to resolve temporal dynamics and adapted computational tools to map clone phenotypes and niches in tissue. Our analyses revealed that cyclophosphamide selectively depletes alloreactive clones, although insufficient early expansion leads to incomplete depletion and severe disease. Severe graft‑versus‑host disease is marked by persistent expansion of alloreactive clones, rewiring of homeostatic cell types and diversification of donor-derived CD8 + clonotypes that acquire Hobit (ZNF683) + tissue‑resident memory T (T RM ) cell programs during migration to epithelium. Spatial deconvolution identified CD8 + effector/Hobit + T RM hubs near intestinal stem‑cell-rich crypt bases and crypt‑loss regions. This clonotype‑resolved framework links tissue‑instructed T RM cell remodeling to localized epithelial injury, nominating early-repertoire dynamics and spatial hub burden as biomarkers.

title: Deletion of a distal IRF4 element prevents inflammation-induced reprogramming of human regulatory T cell fate
abstract: Regulatory T (T reg ) cells in mice can lose lineage identity and acquire proinflammatory functions, but whether human T reg cells are similarly susceptible to cytokine-driven destabilization remains unclear. Here we established an in vitro model of human T reg cell destabilization defined by silencing of the lineage-specifying transcription factor FOXP3, loss of suppressive function and acquisition of proinflammatory activity. Single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic profiling revealed a genome-wide increase in accessibility at AP-1-binding sites, including a putative regulatory element distal to IRF4 . Increased accessibility at this element correlated with increased IRF4 expression during T reg cell destabilization, and its excision conferred resistance to inflammatory cytokine-induced reprogramming. Conversely, forced expression of IRF4 together with BATF promoted T reg cell destabilization. These data identify a distal IRF4 regulatory element as a critical node enabling heightened AP-1-IRF4 cooperative activity to drive T reg cell destabilization, with implications for the design of more stable and effective T reg cell-based therapies.

title: Updating the symbols of ten cytokines and their receptors: report of the IUIS Cytokine Nomenclature Sub-Committee
Metastasis enables immunogenicity through migrasome-mediated antigen release
abstract: Antigen release is a critical step in initiating antitumor immune responses, yet its regulation during metastasis is not well understood. Here we show that circulating tumor cells undergoing vascular migration produce migrasomes that serve as a metastasis-specific mechanism of antigen release. These migrasomes are enriched in tumor-associated antigens, including cancer-testis and mutated antigens, and are captured efficiently by antigen-presenting cells in secondary lymphoid organs, where they undergo cross-presentation to elicit CD8 + T cell-mediated immune responses that constrain metastatic progression. Genetic inhibition of migrasome formation enhances metastasis, while administration of purified cancer-derived migrasomes restores immune-mediated suppression of metastatic growth. These findings show paradoxically that metastasis can enhance tumor immunogenicity through migrasome-mediated antigen release, highlighting a link between cancer dissemination and immune activation and establishing migrasomes as a distinct and potent platform for endogenous tumor antigen delivery.

title: Author Correction: Non-catalytic ubiquitin binding by A20 prevents psoriatic arthritis–like disease and inflammation
Author Correction: Mapping self-associating chromatin hubs identifies Id proteins as key determinants of exhausted CD8+ T cell fate
Author Correction: Exhausted CD8+ T cell fate is programmed by dynamic CTCF-mediated enhancer activation and invariant CTCF-imposed barriers
Remodeling of a distal IRF4 element spurs human regulatory T cell instability under inflammatory conditions
abstract: In an in vitro model, human regulatory T cells undergo inflammatory cytokine-driven reprogramming, resulting in increased chromatin accessibility at AP-1-binding sites, increased IRF4 expression and, ultimately, loss of lineage identity and suppressive function. Deletion of an open chromatin region distal to IRF4 protects cells from this cytokine-induced destabilization.

title: Presenting astrocytes
Line targeting AID
Autoantibody source
Barrier immune memory is programmed by intestinal epithelial cell presentation of cytosol-delivered bacterial antigens
abstract: Antigen compartmentalization is known to influence CD4 and CD8 T cell recognition but its impact on immune responses to different antigens expressed by the same pathogen is poorly understood. By tracking the clonal CD4 T cell response to a single epitope shuttled between different virulence proteins of Citrobacter rodentium , we found that response magnitude and quality depended on antigen localization. Antigens retained within bacteria elicited limited responses, whereas antigens injected into colonocyte cytosol through a type III secretion system generated robust mucosal CD4 T cell responses and promoted formation of epithelial-resident memory T cells. This process required direct presentation by infected epithelial cells. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed that sustained, bidirectional communication between epithelial cells and T cells was essential to elicit both barrier-protective functions and transcriptional programs favoring tissue residency over central memory differentiation. These findings identify nonprofessional antigen-presenting cells as key regulators of CD4 T cell memory fate.

title: Prefibrotic bone marrow microenvironment is a hallmark of clonal hematopoiesis
abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential is associated with systemic inflammation and increased malignant risk in humans, yet understanding of how it reshapes the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment has been limited. Using single-cell transcriptomic profiling of freshly isolated BM samples, combined with histological and spatial transcriptomic analyses, we identified fibro-inflammatory remodeling as a hallmark of clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential. Fibroblasts were markedly expanded and acquired cancer-associated fibroblast-like transcriptional states, while mesenchymal and vascular cells upregulated collagen production and extracellular matrix remodeling pathways. Spatial transcriptomics revealed discrete fiber-enriched regions populated by active and CXCL12 + fibroblasts, macrophages and lymphoid cells. These regions exhibited major enrichment of proinflammatory pathways, including transforming growth factor-beta and tumor necrosis factor signaling, identifying them as spatially confined inflammatory hubs within the BM. Collectively, these findings establish fibro-inflammatory BM remodeling as a defining feature of clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, linking it to prefibrotic stromal changes and niche reorganization that may facilitate progression to overt malignancy.

title: Clonal blood reshapes its home
abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis does more than alter blood cells. Fibroblast-rich inflammatory pockets in bone marrow may help mutant stem cells persist and set the stage for disease.

title: Epithelial antigen presentation shapes barrier memory
abstract: Bacterial antigens injected into the cytosol of intestinal epithelial cells are preferentially presented by MHC II for induction of antigen-specific T cell responses and long-term epithelial cell-associated CD4 tissue-resident memory T cells.

title: Susumu Tonegawa (1939–2026)
Diverse infections transcriptionally reprogram the intestinal epithelium and epithelial–immune cell interactions
authors: on behalf of the MIST Consortium
abstract: The distal small intestine has a vital role in host physiology through its regulation of nutrient and fluid homeostasis. Despite being affected in Crohn’s disease and serving as a major target for a range of infections, we know relatively little about the complexity of cellular responses and cell–cell communication in the ileum during infection. Here we present GutPath, an atlas of over 500,000 single cells with RNA and protein expression profiles for 91 cell states in the ileum across diverse infectious archetypes. We show that GutPath accurately captures established immune responses to infection while revealing pathogen-specific responses in enterocytes. To highlight the discovery potential of this atlas, we identify a new enterocyte transcriptional state present during Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection that is spatially linked to bacterial load and tissue pathology. GutPath establishes a much-needed resource for the immunology community that will accelerate the study of transcriptional diversity in the cellular landscapes of the small intestine.

title: Author Correction: The kinase complex mTORC2 promotes the longevity of virus-specific memory CD4+ T cells by preventing ferroptosis
Zbtb44-mediated transcriptional repression critically regulates colonic inflammation
abstract: The regulatory mechanisms that maintain colonic immune homeostasis remain incompletely understood. Here we show that genetic deletion of Zbtb44 , a previously uncharacterized member of the ZBTB transcription factor family, leads to spontaneous colitis and rectal prolapse. Zbtb44 −/− T cells expressed increased IFN-γ, a pro-inflammatory cytokine strongly associated with human inflammatory bowel disease. Mechanistically, Zbtb44 undergoes SUMOylation, which facilitates its interaction with a conserved SUMO-interacting motif in T-bet, enabling binding to the IFN-γ promoter and enhancer to restrain chronic IFN-γ production. Together, these findings demonstrate that Zbtb44 is a key regulator of colonic inflammation, a role that could be exploited therapeutically.

title: A unique and equity-driven approach to immunology education in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: We present a model for education that has proven transformative for faculty and students, fostering mentorship, inclusion and cross-border collaboration. By embedding training in local contexts, our framework builds confidence, skills and leadership among early-career scientists. These elements foster scientific autonomy and enable sustainable global engagement.

title: Author Correction: Monocyte-derived galectin-1hi cells provide innate immune help in the generation of functional memory CD8+ T cells
Compartment-specific PPARδ activity controls the outcome of cancer–immune cell competition and immunotherapy efficacy
abstract: Most patients with solid tumors fail to sustain antitumor immunity, in part because immune cells cannot outcompete cancer cells inside the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, we show the lipid-sensing transcription factor PPARδ is a compartment-specific determinant of cancer–immune fitness balance and immunotherapy efficacy. Activating PPARδ in cancer cells promotes their growth and impairs antitumor immunity, whereas activating it in immune cells drives tumor suppression and overrides tumor-promoting effects of cancer-intrinsic activation. Mechanistically, PPARδ enhances CD8 + T cell fitness against cancer through effector-associated chromatin remodeling and Cpt1a-mediated fatty acid oxidation. Therapeutically, PPARδ-activated CD8 + T cells sensitize immunotherapy-resistant microsatellite stable metastatic colorectal cancer to checkpoint blockade in mice, and pharmacological or genetic PPARδ activation enhances human chimeric antigen receptor T cell function. These findings identify compartment-specific PPARδ activity as a targetable driver of immune cell fitness that can be harnessed to improve outcomes in immunotherapy-resistant tumors.

title: Evidence for maternal autoantibodies in the pathogenesis of preterm birth
abstract: Preterm birth is associated with breakdown of maternal–fetal tolerance and remains the leading cause of global mortality in young children. However, the role of self-reactive antibodies has been limited to a handful of pathogenic allo- and autoantibodies linked to pregnancy complications. Here we identify a shared autoreactive signature of pregnancy in pregnant sera ( n = 2,719) relative to never-pregnant controls ( n = 130), using proteome-wide autoantibody profiling. Across eight human pregnancy cohorts, we define autoreactivities associated with preterm birth by comparing preterm ( n = 688) and term ( n = 1,505) pregnancies. Within the signature, antibodies to IL1 receptor antagonist (IL1RA) induce resorption, inflammation and vascular malperfusion in pregnant mice. IL1RA localizes to placental endothelial adherens junctions, suggesting a role in vascular integrity. These findings identify a term pregnancy humoral immune program and shared changes preceding preterm delivery, including anti-IL1RA, which may have direct pathogenic consequences.

title: Tuning T cells to give cancer the blues
abstract: On 26–29 May 2026, the first ‘ImmunoMemphis in May’ conference took place at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Memphis, Tennessee, bringing together scientists to catch up on recent advances in T cell immunotherapy.

title: Author Correction: Type A cholesterol-dependent cytolysins translocate to the trans-Golgi network for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
A distinct serological signature of preterm birth
abstract: Preterm birth is the leading cause of death in children globally. We determined proteome-wide autoantibody profiles for 2,195 pregnant individuals, revealing a shared humoral program of normal pregnancy and a distinct, expanded autoreactive signature that precedes preterm birth.

title: The bidirectional double burden of non-communicable diseases and infections
abstract: The alarming rise in NCDs, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, is closely linked to infectious diseases. Despite growing evidence of a bidirectional, mutually reinforcing relationship, these links have received insufficient attention from researchers and healthcare stakeholders.

title: Author Correction: pH sensing controls tissue inflammation by modulating cellular metabolism and endo-lysosomal function of immune cells
Spatial confinement promotes germinal center diversity and tempers immunodominance
abstract: Germinal centers (GCs) form as confined clusters of motile cells within individual lymphoid follicles. The role of confinement in GC B cell evolutionary events is unknown. Here, using mice with reduced GC confinement because of deficiency in Gα13-dependent G-protein-coupled receptor signaling, we observed GC–GC trafficking in confinement-defective lymph nodes (LNs). In multicolor clonal lineage tracing mice, de-confined GCs minimally diversified their color palettes with respect to one another. Spatial B cell receptor sequencing revealed greater clonal crossover between neighboring GCs in the setting of dispersal. The total GC B cell repertoire of LNs with inter-GC exchange also decreased in overall diversity because of increased skewing toward top clones. As an outcome, LNs with de-confined GCs more strongly favored clones responding to accessible epitopes while losing clones binding to other portions of antigen. Together, our findings suggest that confinement supports antibody breadth by moderating the spread of dominant clones and preserving unique trajectories in individual GC responses.

title: A tolerogenic function for gut TFH cells
abstract: Regulatory T (Treg) cells maintain immunological tolerance, but the cellular niches sustaining them across tissues are poorly defined. Work now identifies T follicular helper cells as a source of IL-2 that supports Treg cells in gut-associated lymphoid tissue and promotes intestinal immune homeostasis.

title: A single-cell atlas of human neutrophils reveals neutrophil heterogeneity across health and disease
abstract: Neutrophils, the most abundant leukocytes in human blood, have multifaceted roles in health and disease. Here we assembled a single-cell atlas of human neutrophils (SCAHN) by integrating transcriptome data from 1 million human neutrophils from 781 samples and 43 independent datasets. Using SCAHN, we identified multiple neutrophil subsets with distinct functions across tissues and robust changes in gene expression and subset proportions in infection, cancer, immune suppression and sex differences at single-cell resolution. Cross-species reference mapping of mouse and nonhuman primate neutrophils onto SCAHN revealed both conserved and species-specific features. Using 17,023 bulk blood transcriptome profiles from 40 datasets, we found that neutrophil-specific signatures predicted mortality in acutely ill patients at presentation, were associated with cancer diagnosis and survival, and correlated with metabolic dysfunction and long-term all-cause mortality. Our study highlights how neutrophil biology can improve immune risk stratification and develop effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

title: IL-2-producing TFH cells sustain Treg cell homeostasis and immune tolerance in the gut
abstract: Follicular helper T (T FH ) cells are well known for their role in supporting B cell responses. Here, we identify a critical B cell-independent function for T FH cells in sustaining regulatory T (T reg ) cells within gut-associated lymphoid tissues (GALT). We demonstrate that T FH cells produce interleukin-2 (IL-2) at the T cell–B cell border and within interfollicular regions and that this localized IL-2 is required to maintain GALT T reg cell homeostasis and restrain the expansion of pathogenic effector T cells. Mice selectively lacking IL-2-producing T FH cells develop colitis and fatal multiorgan inflammation, driven by impaired GALT T reg cell responses and uncontrolled effector T cell activation. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment alleviates both intestinal and extraintestinal pathology, indicating that loss of tolerance to commensal-derived antigens is a key driver of disease. Together, these findings define a spatially restricted T FH cell-derived IL-2 niche critical for GALT T reg cell stability and uncover an unexpected immunoregulatory role for T FH cells in maintaining gastrointestinal tolerance beyond B cell help.

title: Serine protease inhibitor A3 is a soluble SIRPα ligand that suppresses inflammation and antitumor immunity
abstract: SIRPα is an inhibitory receptor with the canonical ligand CD47. Here, we show that human serine protease inhibitor A3 (SERPINA3) and its mouse ortholog SERPINA3k function as soluble binders and activators of SIRPα, suppressing SIRPα + macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and natural killer cells. SERPINA3(k) treatment alleviates lipopolysaccharide-induced pneumonia and ameliorates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Although wild-type SERPINA3 provokes inflammation in cardiomyocytes and brain vascular endothelial cells, the SERPINA3D2 mutant, identified through functional domain mapping for SIRPα interaction, abolishes these adverse effects while retaining full inhibitory capacity. Notably, cancer cells secrete large amounts of SERPINA3(k), exceeding CD47 levels. Anti-SERPINA3(k) antibodies, used alone or in combination with blockade of programmed cell death 1 receptor/programmed cell death ligand 1, inhibit tumor growth in multiple preclinical models. This work identifies a potent soluble SIRPα ligand, offering effective therapeutic strategies for inflammatory/autoimmune diseases and a promising target for cancer immunotherapy.

title: Cytokine circuits in CNS homeostasis and disease
abstract: Cytokines are critical regulators of central nervous system (CNS) integrity, acting not only as immune messengers but also as signals that coordinate interactions among glial and neuronal cells, resident macrophages, such as microglia and border-associated macrophages, and infiltrating leukocytes. These circuits establish basal immune tone, shape responses to perturbation, and promote tissue adaptation and recovery. In this Review, we examine selected cytokine pathways across homeostasis, inflammatory or degenerative tissue damage and repair to develop a framework for how cytokine networks preserve, destabilize and restore CNS integrity. We focus on CSF-1, IL-34, TGFβ and IL-33 in homeostasis; IL-1, TNF, GM-CSF and IFNγ in inflammation; type I and II interferons in antiviral and neurodegenerative states; and IL-12 at the interface of innate sensing, adaptive immunity and tissue-protective adaptation. By focusing on instructive modules, we highlight broader organizing principles and how cytokine miscalibration can lead to neurological disease across diverse contexts.

title: GutPath links immune archetypes and single-cell landscapes in the infected gut
abstract: A single-cell gene expression atlas, spanning six phylogenetically diverse infections, reveals pathogen-specific reprogramming of the intestinal epithelium and a novel Yersinia-induced enterocyte state that is spatially linked to tissue pathology.

title: The maternal–fetal interface is an early hematopoietic niche enriched in distinct erythro-myeloid progenitors
abstract: Embryonic hematopoiesis is thought to occur exclusively in the extraembryonic yolk sac before hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) arise in the aorta–gonad–mesonephros region. Here we identify a previously unrecognized hematopoietic site at the maternal–fetal interface in mice, termed MIXER (Maternally Interfaced eXtraEmbRyonic) tissue, which develops contemporaneously with the yolk sac and exhibits robust hematopoietic activity. MIXER contains abundant hematopoietic precursors, including classical CSF1R + erythro-myeloid progenitors and a unique embryonic CD4 + CSF1R − Erythro-Myeloid PRogenitOR (eEMPROR) population. Lineage-tracing experiments demonstrate that eEMPROR cells contribute to select macrophage subpopulations during fetal development, primarily in the perivascular space. Notably, early human placental villi, before HSC emergence, also harbor CD4 + nucleated erythrocytes, indicating a conserved hematopoietic role for the maternal–fetal interface. These findings establish MIXER as an anatomically distinct niche for embryonic hematopoiesis and expand the developmental map of blood cell emergence in mammals.

title: A CD4-lineage erythro–myeloid progenitor within the adult bone marrow defines an alternative pathway for macrophage generation
abstract: Tissue-resident macrophages originate from distinct developmental sources, but their adult replenishment is thought to depend exclusively on circulating monocytes. Here we identify a previously unrecognized CD4-lineage erythro–myeloid progenitor (EMPROR) in the adult bone marrow that provides an alternative pathway for macrophage generation. EMPROR cells are phenotypically and transcriptionally distinct from hematopoietic stem cells, common myeloid progenitors and monocyte precursors, lacking Csf1r and Ccr2 while expressing Cd4 and Kit . Single-cell RNA sequencing, RNA velocity analysis and lineage assays reveal macrophage, neutrophil, megakaryocytic and erythroid potential. EMPROR cells generate perivascular and tumor-associated macrophages independently of CCR2-mediated monocyte recruitment and contribute to erythroid and granulocytic lineages under inflammatory and neoplastic conditions. Transcriptomic comparisons position EMPROR cells closest to embryonic erythro–myeloid progenitors, indicating the persistence of an embryonic-like program in adult bone marrow. These findings reveal an alternative pathway of adult myelopoiesis that sustains macrophage diversity beyond the classical monocyte lineage.

title: The EMPROR’s new groove
abstract: Two studies shed new light on macrophage origins. Perivascular macrophages derive from extraembryonic erythromyeloid progenitors arising at a newly discovered hematopoietic site at the maternal–fetal interface and a related population of adult bone marrow progenitors.

title: TRAM-dependent myddosomes
Autophagy in macrophages curtails IL-1α-mediated immune priming against lung infections
abstract: Host resistance to infection is initially determined by how well primed the innate immune system is to respond on first exposure to an invader, yet the mechanisms underlying this priming remain incompletely understood. Here we found that basal autophagy suppressed the expression of Il1a in alveolar macrophages (AMs) and an otherwise protective innate immune priming against Staphylococcus aureus and influenza A virus (IAV), independently of the microbiome and adaptive immunity. Inactivating autophagy genes in AMs led to elevated expression of IL-1α in AMs, which subsequently enhanced IL-1R-MyD88 signaling in neutrophils and increased the recruitment of myeloid cells to the lung. As a result, autophagy-deficient mice showed more efficient clearance of S. aureus along with reduced lung damage and inflammation. Similar to genetic inactivation of autophagy, overexpression of IL-1α in AMs conferred broad spectrum protection against S. aureus and IAV, suggesting a possible strategy to fine-tune immune responses to combat important respiratory infections.

title: Linda J. Miller (1958–2026)
Autophagy limits steady-state IL-1α expression to restrain innate immunity
abstract: Autophagy controls pulmonary innate immunity at the steady-state by restraining IL-1α expression by alveolar macrophages. Disrupting this regulatory pathway primes lung innate immunity and enhances resistance to distinct respiratory infections, identifying an unexpected role for autophagy in determining host immune readiness.
